We wear harnesses like crossing guards. In a pouch over the heart, over stent and bypass, a black box with leads pressed onto metal nipples. We pedal and tread and row while our signals are picked upby antennas on the ceiling, X’s like the eyes cartoonists give the dead.Angels of telemetry with vials of nitro watch over us. We beam to their monitors now a barn dance, now a moonwalk. They cuff us and pump and we keep on so tomorrow will live off today. Nurse, we won’t forget the animated video of our cholesterol highway where LDL, black-hatted scowling donut holes on wheels, blocked traffic.But with muscles like gutta-percha, can we leave time’s gurney in the dust? In reply, a tape of Little Richard or Jerry Lee comes on and we’re singing, aloud or not, all pale infarcted pedalers, rowers, treadmillers, and our hearts are rising in the east.

outputs.L1:
We wear harnesses like crossing guards. In a pouch over the heart—over stent and bypass—rests a black box, its leads pressed onto metal nipples. We pedal and tread and row while our signals are gathered by antennas on the ceiling, X's like the eyes cartoonists give the dead.

Angels of telemetry, bearing vials of nitro, keep watch over us. To their monitors we beam now a barn dance, now a moonwalk. They cuff us and pump, and still we persist, so that tomorrow may live off today. Nurse, we will not forget the animated video of our cholesterol highway, where LDL—black-hatted, scowling donut holes on wheels—brought traffic to a standstill.

Yet with muscles like gutta-percha, can we leave time's gurney in the dust? By now, only the dead know more of gravity than we do. In reply, a tape of Little Richard or Jerry Lee begins to play, and we are singing—aloud or not—all of us pale, infarcted pedalers, rowers, treadmillers, our hearts rising in the east.
outputs.L2:
Strapped into vests reminiscent of school-zone traffic monitors, we go about our exercises. Positioned above the heart—right over the surgical scars and inserted stents—sits a small dark device, its wires clamped to metallic contact points. As we cycle, walk, and simulate rowing, our transmissions get captured by antennas mounted overhead, marked with X shapes like the crossed-out eyes illustrators sketch onto lifeless cartoon figures.

Guardian figures of the telemetry world, armed with little bottles of nitroglycerin, keep their watchful eyes on us. Our movements broadcast to their screens—one moment resembling a rustic square dance, the next a Michael Jackson glide. They wrap the pressure cuffs around us and squeeze, and still we persist, so that today's effort might purchase us a tomorrow. And Nurse, we'll always recall that cartoon journey through our cholesterol roadways, where the LDL particles—sneering, villain-hatted donut holes rolling along on tiny wheels—jammed the flow of traffic.

Yet with our tissues gone rubbery and stiff, is there any hope of outrunning the stretcher that time has waiting for us? At this point, perhaps only the deceased understand gravity better than we do. As if answering, a recording of Little Richard or Jerry Lee Lewis begins to play, and suddenly we're singing—whether out loud or silently within—every one of us washed-out, heart-damaged cyclists, rowers, and treadmill-walkers, feeling our hearts climb upward like a sunrise on the horizon.

# Cardiac Rehabilitation: Between Machinery and Mortality

In the cardiac rehabilitation center, patients exercise while wearing monitoring harnesses that transmit their heart signals to overhead antennas and staff monitors. These devices translate the private, internal rhythms of each patient's heart into visible data, allowing every beat to be observed and recorded in real time. The technology creates a constant connection between the individuals working to rebuild their strength and those responsible for their care.

Watching over them are the medical personnel, aptly described as "angels of telemetry." With nitroglycerin ready and attentive to each fluctuation in blood pressure, these caregivers stand as guardians dedicated to sustaining the lives entrusted to them. Their vigilance transforms the clinical environment into something almost sacred—a space where human attention and medical readiness work together to hold mortality at bay.

The patients carry with them the memory of an educational animated video that depicted cholesterol in vivid, cautionary terms. In it, menacing LDL particles crowded and blocked the arterial "highway," dramatizing the invisible threats coursing through their own bodies. This imagery lingers, giving concrete form to the dangers they cannot see but now understand all too well.

Yet even as they labor to strengthen their bodies, the patients cannot escape a deeper confrontation. Each session brings them face to face with their own mortality and an intimate, unavoidable awareness of physical decline and death. The exercise is both a hopeful act of renewal and a reminder of fragility—a paradox that shapes every moment spent in the rehabilitation room.

Against this backdrop, music becomes a source of unexpected uplift. The driving rhythms of Little Richard and Jerry Lee Lewis fill the air, inspiring the exercising patients and lifting their spirits. As their bodies move and their pulses quicken, their hearts seem to "rise in the east," symbolically greeting a new dawn of renewed hope. In this fusion of sound, effort, and vigilant care, the patients find not only the will to endure but a fragile, radiant optimism about the days ahead.
outputs.L4:
# Rising Hearts

In a bright room that smells of effort and antiseptic, they gather—the survivors. Men and women who have felt the surgeon's blade, who carry within their chests the small metal scaffolding of stents, or wear beneath their skin the rerouted rivers of bypass grafts. They come here now to walk, to pedal, to lift their arms against the pull of gravity and time.

Each of them is wired. Telemetry harnesses cross their torsos like bandoliers, electrodes pressed against the skin, thin cables gathering the electric whisper of each heartbeat and sending it outward, upward, to the nurses who watch the traveling green lines on their screens. Here are hearts made visible, made public—the most private muscle broadcasting its labor to strangers who read the language of the pulse, who know when a rhythm stumbles, when a chamber falters.

Watch them move. See how the woman on the treadmill sets her jaw, her sneakers finding a rhythm older than her scars. See the man beside her, whose sternum was cracked open and wired shut, now lifting weights that would once have seemed like nothing, now monumental. They are engaged in the oldest negotiation—the body bargaining with its own mortality, each step a small argument against the ending that brushed so close.

They know how fragile they are. They have felt the flutter, the crushing weight, the sudden certainty that the engine might simply stop. They have lain on tables while machines breathed for them. They carry this knowledge now like a stone in the pocket, this intimate acquaintance with their own dissolution.

And yet—

Somewhere a radio plays. Old rock and roll spills into the room, a defiant backbeat, guitars that refuse to apologize. And something rises in them. Their feet quicken. A grin breaks across a weathered face. This is the music of being alive, of being young and reckless and immortal, and though their bodies have betrayed that dream, the spirit in them will not surrender. They move together, these battered pilgrims, drawing strength from one another's presence, from the shared understanding that lives unspoken between them.

On the monitors, the green lines climb. Hearts rising—literally, electrically, and something more. For in those ascending rhythms is the oldest human signal: *not yet, not yet, I am still here.* The rising hearts become a kind of prayer, a flag raised against the dark, the stubborn, luminous insistence of the will to live.
outputs.L5:
# Guardian Angels in White

There's a reason nurses have long been called "angels in white." They move through hospital corridors at all hours, carrying comfort in their hands and compassion in their hearts.

## Silent Heroes

When patients are at their most vulnerable—frightened, in pain, or facing uncertainty—it is often a nurse who provides the first reassuring word. They check on us in the quiet hours of the night when no one else is watching. They notice the small changes that others might miss, and they advocate for us when we cannot speak for ourselves.

## More Than a Job

For a nurse, caregiving is more than a profession; it is a calling. They sacrifice holidays with their own families to sit beside strangers. They hold hands through difficult diagnoses and celebrate quietly when a patient takes their first steps toward recovery. Their work demands both scientific precision and endless kindness.

## The Angels Among Us

We call them angels not because they have wings, but because of what they carry within them: patience during long shifts, strength when others are weak, and hope offered freely to those who have lost their own.

The next time you meet a nurse, remember that you are in the presence of someone who has chosen to spend their life healing others. They are, in every meaningful sense, the guardian angels walking among us—dressed not in feathers, but in scrubs and quiet determination.

*To every nurse: thank you for being the angels this world needs.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about patients in a cardiac rehabilitation program exercising while hooked up to heart monitors, using rich metaphor and dark humor.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Telemetry Ward

We are the wired congregation, the reluctant faithful, pedaling our stationary pilgrimages to nowhere. Each of us trails a leash of colored wires, tethered like balloons to the machines that translate us into mountains and valleys, into the green cursive scrawl of our own continued arguing with death.

Look at us: a gallery of second chances in orthopedic sneakers. My neighbor Frank, whose heart once quit mid-sentence at his daughter's wedding, now grunts through his eighth minute like a man rowing across the Styx and being told, *not today, sir, please remain seated.*

The monitors chirp their small alarms—the sound of a smoke detector with low batteries, if the battery were your life. We have learned to read the room by its beeping. A steady rhythm is a lullaby. A stutter is a rumor. We watch each other's numbers the way we once watched stock tickers, back when we believed the important currency was money.

Somewhere a nurse named Diane says *good, good, keep going,* and we are toddlers again, learning to walk on legs that already know how this story ends. The irony is not lost on us: we spend our whole lives trying to *stop* our hearts from racing—the tax bill, the biopsy, the phone that rings at 3 a.m.—and now they pin ribbons on us for making the damn thing gallop.

We are all connected here, literally, unglamorously, by adhesive and suspicion. Twelve strangers sharing the intimate knowledge of each other's electrical honesty. There are no lies on a heart monitor. It is the last confessional, and it prints receipts.

When my time is up, I peel the electrodes from my chest—that particular tug, that small betrayal of skin—and I am briefly, wonderfully, *unmonitored.* Unobserved. A free man for the length of a hallway.

And I think: this is what we came here to practice. Not the pedaling. The leaving. The unhooking. The walking out into the parking lot where nobody is keeping track of your rhythm anymore, where the only thing measuring your heart is the plain blue indifferent sky, which has been doing this counting all along.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, image-dense piece from the collective "we" perspective of heart attack survivors on treadmills and stationary bikes, weaving in telemetry, cholesterol, and rock 'n' roll.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cardiac Rehab, Third Floor

We are the reassembled, the near-misses, the ones
who felt the elephant sit down on our chests
and lived to tell the fluorescent morning about it.
We arrive in our forgiving shoes, our elastic waistbands,
our bodies rewired and rezoned like flooded neighborhoods
learning to trust the river again.

They clip us to the telemetry, those little gray sparrows
of adhesive and wire, and we walk into the machine's opinion of us—
green lines stuttering their honest cursive across the monitors,
each heartbeat a signature we're relearning how to forge.
*Look,* the nurse says, *there you are,* and points to the proof
that we are still authoring something, still spelling ourselves
in that jagged mountain-range language, that seismograph script.

The treadmills hum their gospel of the endless road going nowhere,
and we go there, faithfully, at 2.5 miles an hour,
sweat beading like the small rebellions of the flesh.
Somebody's earbuds leak Springsteen—*tramps like us*—
and we are, we are, we're born to run
though the running now is measured, metered, monitored,
though our arteries once staged their sudden coups,
those cholesterol barricades, that plaque like winter grease
hardening in the pipes of us until the lights went out.

We speak the new dialect: *ejection fraction, statin, stent.*
We carry nitroglycerin like a lozenge of last resort,
a little sun we could dissolve beneath the tongue.
We have seen the numbers—LDL, the bad cop of the bloodstream—
and we've made our peace, our oatmeal peace, our leafy treaties.

But listen: the stationary bikes are spinning like the wheels
of every car we ever drove too fast in 1974,
and for a moment the drum fill kicks in—somebody's radio,
somebody's youth—and our recovering hearts remember
they were built for this, the four-four thunder,
the backbeat that first taught them how to keep a rhythm.
We pedal toward the version of ourselves who danced,
who smoked on fire escapes, who thought the body
was a promise that would never be recalled.

Now we know better. Now we know the body
is on loan, is leased, is a rented room we've come to love
more fiercely for the eviction notice slipped beneath the door.
So we ride. So we walk our sacred nowhere.
The green lines climb and fall, climb and fall,
and every peak is a small hallelujah, a *still here,*
a chorus we didn't know the words to until we almost lost the song.

We are the survivors, the second-drafters, the encore acts.
Unplug us gently. Tell us the numbers looked good today.
We'll gather our jackets and our humbled, grateful engines
and walk back out into the loud and ordinary world—
that great unmonitored country—
where the radio is always playing,
and our hearts, against all odds, keep time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem that transforms a hospital cardiac ward into something mythic and defiant, referencing angels, gravity, and old rock musicians like Little Richard.
counterfactuals.output:
# Telemetry

They wheel the old gods in on gurneys now, each one wired to a green horizon that will not stop confessing. Listen: the heart is just a drummer who refuses the metronome, who insists on the backbeat, on the *wop-bop-a-loo-bop* stutter that gravity has been trying to arrest since the first cell learned to clench.

Down the corridor, an angel in scrubs adjusts the drip. She has clipped her wings to fit the doorframes—regulation, she shrugs, the ceilings here were built by people who forgot how high a thing might want to go. Behind her, the monitors keep their liturgy. Blip. Blip. The sound of Little Richard hammering a piano that has been dead for years and still won't lie down.

*Gravity,* the cardiologist explains, is only love with nowhere else to fall. It pulls the blood back down. It pulls the singer's pompadour toward the floor and the singer says no, says *shut up,* says builds it higher, a black lacquered tower daring the sky to try something. Every systole is a fist. Every diastole, a mercy. The whole ward is a jukebox someone fed a lifetime's worth of quarters and forgot to turn off.

In bed nine, a man who once sold saxophones is negotiating. Not with death—death is boring, death is a bureaucrat with a clipboard—but with the *rhythm,* with the sacred insolence of continuing. His EKG spikes like a guitar solo nobody asked for and everybody needed. The angel leans close. *You're flatlining beautifully,* she whispers, which is a joke, which is a prayer, which is the same thing here where the difference has been unplugged.

And when the code blue comes—it always comes, it is the chorus—watch how they crowd the bed like fans against a stage, how the paddles charge with that holy hum, how the whole defiant congregation of the dying and the barely-saving screams *CLEAR* at the ceiling, at the low medicinal sky, at gravity itself:

*we are not done, we are not done,*
*the show does not close, only shudders,*
*wop-bop-a-loo-bop,*
*and the heart, that ridiculous little Richard,*
*kicks the bench away*
*and stands.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poem about aging bodies and mortality set in a medical rehab gym, mixing clinical imagery with humor and hope.
counterfactuals.output:
# Physical Therapy, Room 3

The parallel bars gleam like an altar rail
where Mr. Kaminski, eighty-three,
makes his slow communion with gravity,
one shuffling step, then another—
a pilgrim who forgot the destination
but remembers the walking.

Here we are, the assembled parts department:
hip like a rusted hinge,
knee that files complaints with every bend,
a shoulder that only lifts
to half-mast now, saluting
some flag we're too tired to salute back.

The therapist, bright as a nurse in a toothpaste ad,
counts our reps like blessings.
*Ten more,* she chirps, and we groan
the ancient liturgy of the almost-broken,
the *oy* and *good Lord* and *sweet mercy*
that translate, in every tongue, to: *I'm still here.*

Mrs. Delgado races her own reflection
in the mirror-walls, laughing
that she's finally slow enough
to have real conversations with her body,
which spent seventy years
ignoring her requests.

We are learning ourselves backward,
these traitor bones, this stubborn meat—
how to rise from a chair
is now a graduate seminar,
how to grip a fork
a small triumphant Olympics.

And yes, we know where this is going.
The body is a lease, not a deed.
But look: someone brought donut holes,
and Kaminski just reached the end of the bars
and turned around, grinning like a boy
who dared the whole length of the pool.

*Again,* he says.

The most human word.
*Again.*

We lift what we can lift.
We hold the rail.
We keep the appointment.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a densely metaphorical piece of literary writing narrated by cardiac patients who are exercising under electronic surveillance, ending on a note of resilience and resurrection.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Choir of Wired Hearts

We are the congregation of the almost-stopped, gathered each morning in this bright abattoir of second chances, where the treadmills hum their pilgrim hymns and the stationary bicycles pedal toward destinations no map has named. They have laced our chests in copper, sewn small electric spiders to our skin, and now the machines drink our thunder and translate it into green and jagged mountains climbing across the screens.

Watch us walk. We are the men and women who died a little in the night, who felt the fist inside us clench like a miser guarding his last gold, who woke to find the world had grown a second skin of monitors. Our hearts are the old choirs now—cracked bells, reluctant drummers—and we have been sent here to teach them music again.

The nurse who reads our rhythms sits behind her glass like a fortune-teller bent above her tea leaves, except our fate is spelled in voltage, in the small hieroglyphic peaks that spike and settle. She knows the language of our fear. She has watched a hundred graphs go feral, a hundred quiet mutinies of muscle. When she frowns, we feel the temperature of mortality drop against our necks like a draft from an opened door.

*Beat*, we tell ourselves. *Beat, you stubborn tenant. Pay your rent in blood.*

We are the archaeologists of our own ruin, digging back through decades of butter and grievance, of cigarettes smoked on fire escapes while the moon looked away, of angers swallowed whole and left to rot like fruit in the cellar of the chest. Each footfall on this rubber road is a coin dropped into the collection plate of penance. We are trying to buy back the country we squandered—the wide green acreage of a healthy pulse, the untaxed breath.

Around us the wires make their harvest. They gather what we are: the frightened animal, the failing pump, the flickering lamp that will not, will *not* go dark. There is a strange communion in this wiring, a fellowship of the tethered. We are kites now, each of us on our electric string, and someone at the other end refuses to let us drift into that final white sky.

The woman beside us was a swimmer once. She tells us this between the metronome of her breathing—how she once cut through water like a rumor, how the lake accepted her body without argument. Now she walks and the screen behind her paints the story of her striving, and we see it: even here, even wired, even afraid, she is still swimming. The medium has only changed. The current runs through copper now instead of cold clear water, but she is moving through it, she is *moving through it.*

We think of Lazarus, that first alumnus of our strange academy, who felt the stone roll back and the daylight enter like a blade. Did his heart pound so, coming back? Did it stumble on the threshold of the living, unsure of its old choreography? We are all small Lazaruses in polyester, resurrected by the rude mercy of paddles and pills, staggering up from our own tombs to relearn the grammar of the pulse.

And here is the secret the wires cannot measure, the thing that lives in the white space between the peaks: we are not merely surviving. Something in us has been sharpened by the nearness of the end. The apple tastes of Eden now. The ordinary morning arrives gilded. We have shaken hands with the darkness and been sent back with a message we cannot fully speak—only walk, only breathe, only lean into the climbing green mountain of the monitor and make it rise.

Beat, our hearts answer. And beat again.

Listen—the machines are singing us. Every jagged summit on the screen is a flag planted on the peak of one more minute claimed. We are the choir of wired hearts, the almost-gone made present, the extinguished coals that caught a second fire. We walk toward nothing and it turns out nothing was the wrong word all along; we walk toward *more*—more mornings, more quarreling, more coffee gone cold in forgotten cups, more love badly expressed and expressed regardless.

The nurse looks up. She nods. Our rhythms hold.

And we rise, all of us, each on our humming machine—rise the way the sun rises, not because it is unafraid of the night but because rising is simply what it does, again and again, an old resurrection wearing the plain clothes of morning.

We are still here.

We beat. We beat. We beat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
